His scar tissue burned at the memory of the wrong name whispered on a different sea floor. He felt the pressure against his mouth before he saw it—Esther's teeth pressing down on her own inner lip.

"I made a mistake," he said.

Her fingers tightened. "You made a decision."

"A wrong one."

"Both."

Simon opened his mouth to speak and met the force of her anger without words. Esther's eyes stayed locked to his, the pressure of her thumb still on his lip. Only when she pulled it away did he understand her intention—one word had passed between them already.

He took a deep breath.

"I left their names inside," he said.

Esther drew in her breath sharply.

Simon braced himself against the wall, feeling the cold of the concrete through his shirt. A quiet, steady pressure rose from Esther's right hand to his chest, her fingers curling around his ribs. Her other hand went to the side of his face, thumb tracing the line where his jawbone met salt-hardened stubble.

The contact was specific rather than embracing: she was examining a wound she hadn't seen.

"Who?" she asked.

He spoke before the word could turn back to memory. "Marta. And Maria."

The air between them changed. Simon caught her next breath like an anchor.

"Their mother?"

He nodded.

selected.cumulative_completion:
Simon looked away. His hair still had that sea smell. Esther resisted the urge to ask about salt and sun and where he slept under which stars. The drive's seal had broken before any of those questions would matter.

"The data," he said, "was copied."

She raised an eyebrow. "You mean they took the original and left a clone?"

He nodded. "I wanted to confirm."

"By breaking the seal? Without consulting me?" Esther circled around him, keeping his gaze. "What if they had made two copies?"

"Then we still have one."

Esther let out a slow breath. "You said the drive was undamaged when you recovered it."

"It was. Physically intact."

"What did you find on your copy?"

"No evidence of cloning software. Just the original files." Simon touched the damaged seal again. "But I wanted to be sure."

Esther sat on the edge of the bed and crossed her arms. "How much time did we lose verifying that your method was safe?"

"Two days."

She closed her eyes for a moment. When she opened them, she traced the outline of his collarbone with her fingertip. "You spent forty-eight hours alone making this decision."

"I know."

"Do you?"

Simon's hands clenched at his sides. His breath changed. Esther watched as he opened himself to the consequences of his choice.

His breath quickened first, then his pulse. She counted both while watching the small beads of sweat form on his upper lip.

"One," she whispered.

"I had no choice."

"Two."

"The house was compromised."

"Three."

"It wasn't secure."

"Four." Esther traced the outline of his mouth with her finger. "The question I haven't asked yet is: Why is my husband afraid to stay alone in our house?"

"You weren't here."

"Five."

His pulse slowed again. Esther removed her hand, leaving wet marks on his skin where it had been.

"Let me be specific," she said. "I have been absent before. Why this time?"

"Because you were gone longer than usual." His hand closed over the drive. "You're never gone this long."

She touched his temple where a single strand of hair had gone white since their last meeting. "Is there another reason I haven't thought to ask?"

He turned toward her touch. "I missed you," he said. "More than usual."

Esther caught his jaw in one hand and kissed him briefly. She traced the old scar where a bullet had taken bone, her lips lingering as if testing its shape.

"Is it possible to have too many reasons?" he asked against her mouth.

selected.cumulative_completion:
Simon pulled back, reached for the tea cup. He drank. The cup shook in his hands.

"Esther—"

"Answer me first."

"I had to copy."

She dropped the remaining button and moved close, her palm against his sternum. "Because I hadn't said yes?"

"We needed time," he said, but didn't look away when she waited.

Esther exhaled through her nose. "I made that decision alone last night," she said, tracing a fresh scar under his shirt. "While you were unconscious."

He moved the tea cup away.

"You didn't wait," she said. "So you made another plan."

"I was afraid you would leave," Simon said, "without me."

She kept her hand against his chest. "Now we'll both stay up all night opening and closing boxes."

He ran a thumb along her jawline. "We will verify the data before dawn."

"Yes." She pressed her palm harder for a moment. "Then I'll tell you what I decided. And then—"

Esther stopped and waited. Simon understood. He bent to kiss her, soft first, then deeper when she opened to him.

"Esther," he murmured between kisses, "may I—"

"Yes." Her hands came up to unbutton his shirt, one at a time, deliberate.

When she reached the fourth button, she stopped and looked directly at him.

"Still yes?"
